## Computing review

### Exercise 7

```{r}
ikea <- read_csv("data/ikea.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: ex-07

ggplot(data = ikea, aes(x = price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x = "price in usd",
       y = "number", 
       title = "The distribution of price in usd")

```

\pagebreak

### Exercise 8

The distribution is skewed to the left, and there are some outliers that will affect the mean to be larger than the median.

### Exercise 9

```{r}
ikea_sub <- ikea |>
  filter(category %in% c( "Sofas & armchairs",
                       "Bookcases & shelving units"))

ikea_sub <- ikea_sub |>
  drop_na(width, price_usd)
```

a\. There is 765 observations in ikea_sub dataframe, and there are 13 variables.

b\. The advantage of complete case analysis is it made further operations more convenient so that there won't be any errors. A disadvantage of complete case analysis is that it might drop out too many elements so that it creates a biased result.

\pagebreak

### Exercise 10

```{r}
#| label: plot-exercise-10
#| fig-cap: "The dataset shows a relatively positive relationship between width and price in usd."
ggplot(data = ikea_sub, aes(x = width, y = price_usd))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "price in usd",
       y = "width")
```

```{r}
#| label: ex-10-colored
#| fig-cap: "Both categories shows a relatively positive relationship between price in usd and width, but the sofas & armchairs category shows a steeper slope, meaning a greater change in price when the width changes."
ggplot(data = ikea_sub, aes(x = width, y = price_usd, color = category, shape = category))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "price in usd",
       y = "width")
```
